prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

cymothoa exigua*: the tongue as what it is not—blemish and parasite: gimp and glottal stop: what question can be answered with a truant mouth: can the lynched man hung from the sails of a windmill taste the lead pipe wedged between his lips: when the signifiers dangle, empty chum lines in a cold creek: when the men in Waco, wearing white straw hats, fraying at the crisp edges of their white shirts, leave Jesse, leave John, leave Paul in ashes in the unpaved streets to choke passing mules into prophecy: when we pinch our noses to staunch the smell of the twice burnt black man burning for a third time this day: when the boys, sweet and good animals, come to what’s been left in shallow ditches: false rib and femur, clavicle and severed hand—quite simply, the language of sorrow: glyph of the gadfly rooting himself into the rotting meat of the dead: when it is too late to refuse our bodies being made urns: corn, unharvested and heavy in its husks: when, in the marketplace, the butcher lifts our tongue from a bed of ice, shouts: who will speak for this flesh: when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Waco, Jesse, John

outputs.L1: *Cymothoa exigua*: the tongue as what it is not—blemish and parasite; gimp and glottal stop. What question can be answered with a truant mouth? Can the lynched man, hanged from the sails of a windmill, taste the lead pipe wedged between his lips? When the signifiers dangle—empty chum lines in a cold creek; when the men in Waco, wearing white straw hats, the crisp edges of their white shirts fraying, leave Jesse, leave John, leave Paul in ashes in the unpaved streets to choke passing mules into prophecy; when we pinch our noses to staunch the smell of the twice-burnt Black man burning for a third time this day; when the boys, sweet and good animals, come upon what has been left in shallow ditches—false rib and femur, clavicle and severed hand—quite simply, the language of sorrow; glyph of the gadfly rooting himself in the rotting meat of the dead; when it is too late to refuse our bodies being made urns; corn, unharvested and heavy in its husks; when, in the marketplace, the butcher lifts our tongue from a bed of ice and shouts, “Who will speak for this flesh?”; when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:
outputs.L2: *Cymothoa exigua*: a tongue mistaken for itself, yet truly a wound, an intruder; a limp paired with a catch in the throat. What inquiry could a missing mouth resolve? Does the lynched man, suspended from a windmill’s blades, still taste the lead pipe forced between his lips? Meaning hangs loose, like baitless fishing lines over an icy stream. In Waco, men in white straw hats and immaculate shirts beginning to unravel abandon Jesse, John, and Paul as ash upon dirt roads, where passing mules cough themselves into omens. We hold our noses against the reek of the Black man who, already burned twice, is set aflame for the third time today. The boys—gentle, decent creatures—approach what remains in shallow trenches: a counterfeit rib, a thighbone, a collarbone, a hand cut away; nothing less than grief’s vocabulary. A gadfly’s mark burrows into the spoiled flesh of the corpse. By the time we understand, we can no longer prevent our bodies from becoming vessels for ashes. Corn stands ungathered, its weighted ears enclosed in husks. At the market, a butcher raises our tongue from its cradle of ice and calls out, “Who will give voice to this meat?” The tongue replies in the only manner available to every tongue severed from its body:
outputs.L3:
The tongue is portrayed simultaneously as a parasite and an absence, symbolizing a capacity for speech that has been damaged, silenced, or violently removed. This image is set alongside graphic depictions of lynching and burned Black bodies, forcing the reader to confront the recurring brutality of racist violence rather than treating it as a distant or abstract historical fact. In the face of such mutilation, words become empty or severed signifiers: language can point toward suffering, but it cannot fully express the sorrow preserved in violated remains.

As a result, the dead body becomes an unwilling vessel of memory, testimony, and even prophecy. Although it bears material evidence of violence, it cannot control how that evidence is interpreted or communicated. The butcher’s question—“who will speak for this flesh”—captures this central dilemma. It asks who has the right or ability to testify on behalf of the dead while emphasizing that no act of representation can restore the voice that violence has severed. The flesh may bear witness, but its testimony remains incomplete, exposing both the necessity and the impossibility of speaking for those who have been forcibly silenced.
outputs.L4:
The text uses visceral, surreal imagery to examine the relationship between racial violence, language, and the Black body. At its center is *Cymothoa exigua*, a parasite that enters a fish through its gills, destroys the fish’s tongue, and then takes the tongue’s place. This grotesque natural process becomes a metaphor for the way racial terror does not merely silence its victims but occupies the space left by that silencing. The parasite embodies a violence that consumes speech while impersonating it, replacing the victim’s voice with the logic and language of oppression.

Images of lynching, mutilation, and burning intensify this metaphor. In these scenes, violence is directed not only at life but also at the body’s capacity to speak, signify, and belong to itself. The tongue—an organ of speech, taste, memory, and identity—becomes especially important. To cut it out is to attempt to sever a person from testimony and to prevent suffering from being named. Yet the text refuses the idea that silence means absence. Even when language is forcibly taken away, the wounded body continues to communicate. Scars, burns, missing limbs, and exposed flesh become forms of evidence: a terrible archive written directly upon the body.

The surreal quality of the imagery allows historical and bodily realities to merge. Human flesh and parasitic life, speech and injury, death and continued witness become difficult to separate. This instability reflects the enduring effects of racial violence, which persist beyond the immediate act and shape how history is remembered—or deliberately forgotten. The mutilated body is made into a spectacle by those who enact violence, but the text reclaims that spectacle as testimony. What was intended to degrade or erase the victim instead indicts the perpetrators and the society that enabled them.

Sorrow therefore becomes embodied rather than merely spoken. It resides in wounds, remains, inherited memories, and the silence surrounding historical atrocity. The severed tongue cannot speak in an ordinary sense, but its absence speaks powerfully. It reveals both the brutality of the attempt to suppress Black expression and the impossibility of fully accomplishing that suppression. Like the parasite that takes the tongue’s place, history may distort, consume, or appropriate the voices of the dead. Nevertheless, the wounds retain their own meaning.

Ultimately, the text presents the Black body as an unwilling but enduring historical record. Flesh bears witness when official language fails, when archives exclude, and when victims are denied the chance to tell their own stories. The body’s sorrow survives as accusation and memory. Even silenced, severed, or burned, it continues to testify against the violence that sought to make it disappear.
outputs.L5: In the heart of **Waco**, where history and modern life meet, **Jesse** and **John** began a journey they would never forget. What started as a simple visit soon became an exploration of the city’s landmarks, culture, and complicated past. As they walked along the Brazos River and spoke with local residents, Jesse and John discovered that Waco was more than its reputation—it was a community shaped by resilience, change, and hope for the future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem titled “cymothoa exigua” that uses the tongue-eating louse as a metaphor for racial violence, silencing, and the failure of language. Use long, colon-linked clauses and end with a severed tongue being asked to speak.
counterfactuals.output:
# cymothoa exigua

It enters by the gill: by the side-door history leaves unguarded: a pale republic of legs: a small hunger fastening itself where breath becomes voice: and the fish goes on shining beneath the surface as if nothing has happened: as if the sea were not already salted with names refused burial: as if a mouth could lose its witness and still be called whole:

First it drinks from the tongue: then the tongue withers: then the parasite takes its place: such is the grammar of racial violence: not merely to strike the word from the mouth but to inhabit the wound: to make the wound pronounce the master’s weather: benevolent rain: incidental thunder: a few dark clouds moving elsewhere:

The fish eats with the thing that ate its speech: the nation speaks with the thing that fed on its dead: law opening and closing its borrowed mouth: archive scraping its many feet across the palate: every sentence wearing the uniform of passive voice: was stopped: was found: was feared: was fired upon: the hand erased so the bullet might appear self-born:

And what can language do when language is the decoy tongue: when justice is a sound made by mandibles: when equality clicks inside the mouth that cannot taste it: we say history because the blood has dried: we say incident because the body was singular: we say unrest because the streets remember what the textbooks cauterized: we say silence though silence is never empty: it is packed tight with swallowed sirens: with mothers naming children into cameras: with children learning how not to move:

O cymothoa: little colonizer: pale apostrophe nailed to the root: you do not forbid speech: you become its instrument: you teach the captive mouth to mistake survival for consent: you make the fish complicit in its own hunger: you make us ask whether a voice is still a voice when every word must pass through the body of what consumed it:

Yet beneath each fluent lie the vanished muscle keeps its red grammar: nerve remembering nerve: taste remembering salt: a sentence spasming where no sentence can be formed: and on the shore, beside the official microphone, someone lifts the severed tongue in both hands and asks it to speak.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, surreal poem about lynching and the Black body, weaving together images of mouths, parasites, butchered flesh, bones, cornfields, and historical violence in Waco. Make the syntax fragmented, incantatory, and unrelenting.
counterfactuals.output:
**Waco Mouth**

May, nineteen-sixteen—  
the courthouse opened its white mouth.  
The square opened another.  
Windows, balconies, rooftops: teeth.  
Ten thousand tongues chanting  
fire, fire,  
as if fire were law,  
as if law had not already buttoned  
its butcher’s apron.

Jesse Washington, seventeen—  
a name dragged through dust,  
a Black body made public grammar:  
rope for verb,  
flame for period,  
the crowd conjugating death  
until every mouth was red.

O mouth of Waco.  
O iron throat.  
O postcard sun  
licking the char from the afternoon.

Parasites flowered in the rafters—  
camera-eyes, coin-fingers,  
men pocketing bone,  
children lifted above shoulders  
to see what history eats.

And history eats.

It eats the wrist,  
the kneecap,  
the soft architecture of breath.  
It gnaws the name from the name.  
It salts butchered flesh  
with hymns.  
It calls the carcass evidence.  
It calls the cheering innocent.

Beyond the square, cornfields  
stood in their green uniforms,  
each stalk hiding a blade,  
each ear packed with pale teeth.  
Wind moved through them—

hush, hush—

but there was no hush.  
Only the rope’s dry psalm.  
Only fat in the fire.  
Only bones becoming bells  
no church would ring.

Black body, black body—  
not symbol.  
Not harvest.  
Not meat beneath the state’s bright hook.

Yet the mouths came crawling,  
fly-mouth, judge-mouth,  
newspaper-mouth, mother-mouth,  
each carrying a small white worm  
called forgetting.

They fed it photographs.  
They fed it ash.  
They fed it the lie  
that nobody could be guilty  
when everybody watched.

Waco: a wound with streets.  
Waco: a furnace wearing Sunday clothes.  
Waco: corn silk caught  
in the teeth of the dead.

And under the earth  
the bones do not sleep.

They knock.  
They knock beneath courthouses,  
beneath statues, beneath the clean plates  
of the descendants.

They say the name.

Jesse.

They say the body.

Black.

They say the crime.

America.

Again—  
the mouth.  
Again—  
the rope.  
Again—  
the crowd flowering like mold  
around the butchered hour.

And still the bones knock.

Not mercy.

Not silence.

A door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph prose poem in the style of a contemporary avant-garde elegy. Begin with “cymothoa exigua*:” and explore what happens when language is forced to inhabit the wounds of the dead. Avoid conventional sentences and rely heavily on colons.
counterfactuals.output: cymothoa exigua*: language entering the wound as a tenant enters a condemned house: no furniture but salt: no window but the memory of seeing: each noun fastening its small white mouth to the vanished tongue: mother: brother: beloved: titles for rooms where the blood has already packed its bags: and grammar, poor parasite, feeding on the silence it replaces: saying body when it means door: saying gone when it means everywhere without shelter: the dead opening inside each syllable: not resurrection: occupation: not song: the thin machinery of breath rehearsing a name until the name becomes scar tissue: until the scar speaks: until what speaks is neither ours nor theirs but the wound wearing language like a borrowed face: luminous: unbearable: still hungry
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a visceral meditation on the question “Who will speak for this flesh?” Include a tongue displayed on ice in a marketplace, white men leaving Black victims in the street, twice-burned bodies, shallow ditches, and anatomy rendered as a sorrowful alphabet.
counterfactuals.output:
Who will speak for this flesh?

The tongue lies displayed on ice in the marketplace, dark muscle among silver fish, tagged with no name, priced beyond grief. Once it shaped a mother’s syllables. Once it pressed laughter against the roof of a mouth. Now shoppers pass beneath the fluorescent hum, and no one asks what word was severed halfway through.

Who will speak for this flesh when the mouth has been made evidence?

White men leave Black victims in the street and call the street empty. They step around the bodies as though around rainwater, carrying clean cuffs, clean stories, clean verdicts. Behind them, blood enters the cracks in the pavement and begins its long testimony. The city washes its hands. The gutters remember.

There are twice-burned bodies: first by flame, then by forgetting. Fire takes the face; silence takes the name. What remains is shoveled into shallow ditches where earth is expected to become an accomplice. But soil has its own archive. Roots touch bone. Worms turn the smallest fragments toward morning. Even buried, the body declines to disappear.

Who will speak?

The anatomy assembles itself into a sorrowful alphabet:  
A is the arm raised too late.  
B is the back carrying history’s bootprint.  
C is the curled hand.  
D is the ditch.  
E is the eye kept open by terror.  
F is flesh, made fact, made flag, made forbidden text.  
G is the gap where a name should be.  
H is the heart, still accused of beating.  

Every rib is a bracket around an unfinished sentence. Every tooth is punctuation. The spine is a blackened exclamation no official report can straighten. The skull, emptied of its dreams, becomes a bowl holding the echo of a question.

Who will speak for this flesh?

Not pity alone. Pity watches from a safe distance. Not history alone. History is too often written by the hand that struck the match. Let the living speak, but let them speak without stealing the dead into metaphor. Let them say: this tongue belonged to someone. This ash had a birthday. These bones were embraced. This blood traveled beneath skin warm from sleep.

And let the flesh speak in its own ruined grammar: the bruise, the blister, the wound that refuses the passive voice. Let the ditch open its dark mouth. Let the marketplace thaw. Let every letter of the sorrowful alphabet rise from the body and enter ours.

Until silence itself is forced to testify.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dense, image-driven anti-lynching poem in which the tongue is simultaneously organ, parasite, absence, and failed witness. Use grotesque historical imagery, rhetorical questions, biblical undertones, and a final unfinished clause that ends after “when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:”.
counterfactuals.output:
The tongue wakes nailed beneath the teeth,  
a red apostle sweating in its cave,  
while outside, the courthouse clock chews midnight  
and white hands braid the hemp like scripture.

What did the sycamore testify  
but weight? What did the lanterns learn  
from a face unmade by flame,  
from shoes turning slowly above the hymnals,  
from the crowd’s bright picnic of teeth?

The tongue, that leech in the mouth,  
fattens on iron, drinks the last name backward,  
curls from the smoke as if to flee its owner—  
yet cannot crawl beyond the jaw.

O witness without a witness stand,  
where was your word when the sheriff opened the gate,  
when children were lifted to see,  
when postcards trapped the dead in silver salt  
and mothers received the image stamped *Wish you were here*?

No cock crowed. No veil tore.  
Only the shutter blinked its one cold eye.  
Only the branch, bent like a question,  
held its black fruit against the dawn.

They cut the tongue out afterward—  
or said they did—  
and sold its silence by the inch.  
But absence has roots. Absence nests  
behind every courthouse Bible,  
hatches flies in the margin beside *Thou shalt not kill.*

Is the tongue an organ if it cannot name the knife?  
A parasite if it survives by swallowing terror?  
An absence if every mouth inherits the wound?  
A witness if its testimony is smoke?

Listen: beneath the ash, something wet keeps pleading.  
Listen: the earth has many mouths and no acquittal.  
Listen, Lord—if Lord is not another locked door—  
to the rope creaking amen above the road,  
to the blood spelling nothing the jury will read,

when the tongue answers as all severed tongues do:
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
